title: Is Contemporary Leadership Advice Really Just B.S.?
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This Admired Leadership piece responds to Jeffrey Pfeffer's book Leadership BS, which argues that successful business leaders often do the opposite of conventional leadership advice, being untrustworthy, inauthentic, and prone to tirades. The author grants that Pfeffer builds a strong case but identifies a common mistake: treating leadership and financial success as cause and effect. Great leadership, the piece argues, does not guarantee business results; it creates the individual and team performance that makes success possible and makes organizations deserving of it. Many factors beyond anyone's control determine outcomes, so organizations can succeed despite poor leadership or fail despite great leadership. The closing move broadens the definition of success beyond dollars and cents, arguing that quality leadership matters most for winning at life.
points: Pfeffer's claims, that successful leaders are often untrustworthy, inauthentic, and emotionally volatile, are summarized as the challenge to conventional advice.
The core rebuttal is that Pfeffer wrongly treats leadership and financial success as cause and effect.
Leaders don't determine financial success; they shape the environment where many forms of success have the best chance, as a competitor's superior product can still sink a well-led firm.
Without great leadership, the piece argues, success collapses into a one-dimensional measure of money.
quotes: Renowned Stanford Business Professor Jeffrey Pfeffer wrote a doozy of a book in 2015 entitled Leadership BS. It seems some titles create more noise years after publication, and that appears to be the case with Pfeffer’s book. It is getting some play once again in small and large organizations.

The chapters inside the book claim contemporary leadership advice gets it all wrong. Successful business leaders, Pfeffer attempts to prove through a series of research studies and anecdotal examples, do the opposite of what is generally thought to be effective.
Pfeffer builds a strong case, but makes a common mistake. He presumes leadership and financial success are both cause and effect.
Great leadership doesn’t guarantee business or financial success. Instead, it promises to create the individual and team performance essential for that possibility.

Leaders don’t determine financial or business success. Instead, they influence the environment where many forms of success, not only the financial ones, have the greatest chance of becoming a reality.
Winning the lottery doesn’t require great leadership. It just requires a ticket. Winning at life, on the other hand, depends heavily on quality leadership.
